brief.subject: Fake debt collectors halted, plus rental and car pricing tricks
brief.headline: Court Freezes Phantom Debt Collector; FTC Targets Hidden Rent and Car Fees
brief.dek: A court halted a debt operation accused of chasing debts people didn't owe, and the FTC settled two hidden-pricing cases.
brief.lede: At the FTC's request, a federal court has stopped and frozen the assets of a debt collection operation accused of pressuring people to pay debts they often didn't owe.

sections.heading: Phantom debt collector shut down
bullets: A federal court has temporarily halted the operation and frozen its assets, according to the FTC.
The collectors allegedly posed as lawyers or attorney-affiliated firms to scare people into paying.
They allegedly threatened to contact victims' employers and relatives, a classic pressure tactic.
If a collector calls, ask for written proof of the debt before you pay anything.

sections.heading: $49.75 million rental pricing settlement
bullets: Progress Residential and owner Pretium Partners will pay $49.75 million to settle FTC charges joined by four states.
The FTC alleges the firms misled renters about what homes would actually cost.
Progress is the largest single-family rental manager in the U.S., so many households could be affected.
The FTC calls it its largest enforcement action ever against a landlord.

sections.heading: Car dealer's low prices weren't real
bullets: The FTC settled with Stream Auto Outlet, a dealership group based on Long Island, New York.
Regulators say it advertised prices far below what buyers ended up paying.
Before signing, ask the dealer for a written out-the-door price that includes every fee.

brief.seo_description: Court freezes a phantom debt collector posing as lawyers; FTC wins $49.75 million rental settlement and a car dealer pricing deal.

items.title: Progress Residential and Owner Pretium Partners to Pay $49.75 Million to Settle FTC and States’ Charges Over Deceptive Rental Pricing Practices and Other Unlawful Conduct
items.snippet: The nation’s largest property manager of single-family rental homes, Progress Residential, and its owner, private equity firm Pretium Partners, will pay $49.75 million to settle charges brought by the Federal Trade Commission and four states that the companies misled consumers with deceptive rental pricing practices.
